text: A love affair carried on in a city being bombed by night and emptied of Jews by day. Berlin, 1943. One of the two women works with the underground; the other is held up as a model of German motherhood, with the household and the children to prove it, so whatever passes between them has to be fitted around husbands, papers, children and the air-raid schedule. That domestic scale is the risk Max Färberböck takes: the war arrives as interruption rather than spectacle, and the danger is administrative before it is dramatic. A Silver Bear went to the leading performance, which is where the film's weight belongs, on a face calculating in real time how much can be said aloud. Sentiment would be the easy road through material like this, and across 125 minutes the picture keeps declining it.

A man of fifty-one, twenty months out of work, takes the job he is offered and only later finds out what it asks of him. Stéphane Brizé builds the film out of that gap. Thierry needs the wage; the wage comes with conditions he did not negotiate and cannot appeal; and at ninety-three minutes there is no room for a second story to relieve the first. The European Film Award went to the lead, for a performance that is largely listening, sitting through rooms in which the terms are explained to him by people who are themselves following instructions. What makes it hard to shake off is that the moral question never announces itself as one. It arrives as a shift, a task, a piece of standard practice that would be unremarkable if he had savings.

Two explanations are available for what is happening to Michaela, and the film declines to choose. She is epileptic and she is devout. She leaves home for college, stops taking her medication, and begins hearing voices that instruct a Catholic girl to keep away from religious objects; one priest scoffs at the idea of possession, and a younger one is willing to act. Hans-Christian Schmid stages this as domestic drama and nothing else, so nothing in the filmmaking arrives to settle the question on the audience's behalf. The European Film Award for Best Actress went to a performance that has to hold both readings at once. What lingers across ninety-two minutes is the reasonableness of everyone involved: believers and sceptics alike sound patient, careful and entirely sure.

An American scholar turns up in Greece with a theory of improvement and a woman he intends to try it on. He is infatuated with her. She sells sex and appears to have decided some time ago that her life suits her. Jules Dassin shot the film in Greece and in Greek, which matters more than a credit line suggests, since the comedy only works if the life being corrected is filmed as a whole world rather than as scenery for a visitor's project. Ninety-one minutes, and the blade stays pointed at the man holding the syllabus, whose conviction is sincere and whose taste is not bad; he simply cannot conceive of being turned down. It was made in 1960, when an American abroad could assume that authority without being asked to defend it. Nobody here is stupid, which is why the argument stays funny.

Abortion pays better than anything else available to a mother of two in occupied France. Marie Latour is not a resister and not a martyr. She performs the procedures at home, rents a spare room to a prostitute she knows, spends what comes in, and gives her injured husband about the attention she can spare once everything else is done. There is a young lover as well, taken chiefly against boredom. Claude Chabrol films all of it without arranging anyone's sympathies. The occupation is weather here, constant and low, and the scandal of the period is always somebody else's business; the money, meanwhile, is real and improves things. The César that went to the lead is for exactly that refusal: no apology, no defiance, no plea. 108 minutes at kitchen height, which is precisely the wrong distance for comfort.

The beach house is ugly and half broken, and that is before the relatives arrive. Roger Hobbs, a banker, wanted two weeks alone with his wife; what he gets is a rented place on the California coast, a daughter who will not be seen in public because of her braces, a son who has brought his television habit along, and then two grown daughters and the husbands they are unhappy with. Henry Koster runs it at a hundred and sixteen minutes, which is a long stay, and the length is the point. The vacation is a job and the father is staff. American family comedy in 1962 held that a man could repair all this by taking each problem in the right order, and the film is straight-faced enough about that to let the labour show. The comedy is in the noise: a household at close quarters, nobody cruel, everybody impossible.

Eighty minutes, two people, and an arrangement made before either of them arrives. She has a fantasy, she has found a man willing to meet her for it, and that is the whole of the premise; Frédéric Fonteyne is plainly less interested in the act than in everything that has to be agreed, timed and got through around it. The scale is small enough that the film has nowhere to hide. A Belgian production, in French, from 1999. Two adults are careful with each other, and the pressure comes from a plain property of transactions, which is that they provide no vocabulary for whatever else may be happening inside them. The European Film Award for Best Actress recognised the harder half of that: a woman keeping track of how much of herself the arrangement covers.

Two addresses: a flat in the suburbs with a possessive man in it, and a small place in Paris kept for the weekends. She intends to have both, and Éric Rohmer spends 102 minutes on that arrangement being explained, defended and tested against other people's plans. His characters talk with unusual fluency, which is the pleasure of the film and also its trap, since an argument made that well can hide its cost from the person making it. The suburbs are filmed as a place where people live rather than as a punchline, and the parties are filmed without envy, so there is no thumb on the scale once the weekends begin to cost something. A César went to the lead, for a performance that has to be persuasive and slightly wrong at the same time. Almost nothing happens loudly, and what matters is audible in the way a sentence gets finished.

Everything is arranged around one trick, called the triple, that two men on a trapeze intend to complete. That is a useful thing for a story to own: a goal that can be seen, timed and failed in front of a paying audience. Carol Reed treats the circus as a place of work rather than of wonder, with practice, hierarchy and the standing question of who catches whom, and then admits a woman to the act, at which point the arithmetic of a pair stops working. Physical risk and jealousy are usually separate engines. Here they run on one shaft, because the man in the air has to trust hands whose reasons have changed since last week. An American production of 1956, 105 minutes, and the tension can be measured in grip and timing rather than announced.

Turin to Naples, one week, and a blind captain who has no intention of being handled. The young man walking him south is an army cadet doing as he is told, and that asymmetry, one who cannot see and one who cannot refuse, gives Dino Risi a comedy that keeps drawing blood. The captain is rude on purpose and rude with skill. He wants service without pity and has been assigned a boy too junior to withhold either. Cannes gave its acting prize to that performance, and it is built out of tempo: the timing of an insult, the pause before an order. Italy in 1974 supplies the rest, a country crossed at ground level by two men in uniform who cannot speak to each other as equals. 103 minutes structured like an itinerary, each stop costing somebody something.

A nineteen-year-old is sent to a women's prison for a single mistake, and the film goes in with her and stays. What an American picture could show in 1950 was limited, so John Cromwell works with what an institution supplies for free: routine, hierarchy, and the arithmetic of who owes a favour to whom. It is filed as a crime film. The crime it is interested in is administrative, an intake process that receives a frightened girl and returns something more convenient to itself. The Academy noticed the lead performance, whose difficulty is that it has to register change without ever announcing it. Ninety-six minutes, almost all of it inside, and the pressure is cumulative rather than dramatic; nothing that happens to her is happening for the first time in that building.

A woman decides that one of the most powerful gangsters in Manhattan can be told no. Ninety-six minutes, and the interesting part is not the decision but the accounting that follows it: who else becomes exposed, who gets paid, which room the pressure turns up in. Lloyd Bacon keeps the criminal operation looking like an operation, with staff and overheads and a chain of command, which is what makes her position legible. She is not an outsider taking a stand. She is an employee giving notice. In 1937 an American studio could only gesture at what her employment consists of, and the gesturing does something to the film: everyone speaks in euphemism, and the euphemism is not coyness but the sound of people who know exactly what they have agreed to and agreed to it long ago.

A four-year-old with her arm in a cast is told, in several incompatible ways, where her mother has gone. The car accident that broke the arm killed the mother; the father leaves her with an aunt and the aunt's children; the explanations begin. Jacques Doillon films almost all of it at her height, and the effect is not sweet. Adults enter the frame from above with heaven and patience and time, then leave with nothing settled. The other children at school have theories of their own, delivered with total confidence and some of them cruel. She goes on hoping her mother will come back, out loud and in private, and ninety-seven minutes is long enough for that hoping to stop looking like a phase and start looking like an argument she is assembling. It asks more of a small child than most films dare ask of adults.

Peacetime is the problem: a Scottish battalion with nothing left to fight is handed a new commanding officer. The man he replaces is still there every evening, loud and popular, drinking in the mess with officers who used to answer to him. Ronald Neame keeps the whole thing indoors, where a regiment's real weapons are seating plans, dress codes, the timing of a joke and the exact warmth of a greeting. Both men have a case. Barrow is entitled to the discipline he asks for; Sinclair led these soldiers through a war and cannot make himself small in front of them. The Academy recognised the adapted screenplay, which earns it on structure: 106 minutes of escalation in which each separate act of sabotage is too minor to report. Rank turns out to be the least of what is being fought over.
